cover.title: NOAA STILL CAN'T EXPLAIN THIS SOUND

comment: Comment BLOOP if you think it was alive

lines.text: In 1997, the U.S. government recorded a sound in the ocean... so loud, microphones more than 3,000 miles apart all picked it up.
Turn your sound up. This is the real recording.

listen.label: "THE BLOOP"  ·  1997
listen.credit: Audio: NOAA PMEL Acoustics Program / public domain

lines.text: They called it The Bloop. NOAA's underwater microphones were listening for undersea volcanoes in the remote South Pacific.
That network grew out of a Navy system built during the Cold War... to hunt Soviet submarines.
The Bloop rose in pitch for about a minute. It was one of the loudest sounds ever recorded underwater... louder than any animal we know of.
And it came from near the spot where H.P. Lovecraft placed the sunken city of Cthulhu.
For years, people believed something enormous was alive down there.
So NOAA kept moving their microphones closer to Antarctica... and they heard it again. And again.
The Bloop wasn't a creature. It was ice. A massive iceberg, cracking apart.
This is a real iceberg breaking apart, recorded by NOAA.

listen.label: ICEBERG CALVING
listen.credit: Audio: NOAA PMEL Acoustics Program / public domain

lines.text: Icebergs even hum. When one grinds against the sea floor, or another iceberg... it sounds like this.

listen.label: ICEBERG HUM
listen.credit: Audio: NOAA PMEL Acoustics Program / public domain

lines.text: In 1999, NOAA caught another one. They called it Julia... because it sounded like a woman's muffled voice.

listen.label: "JULIA"  ·  MARCH 1, 1999
listen.credit: Audio: NOAA PMEL Acoustics Program / public domain

lines.text: Julia turned out to be a giant iceberg running aground off Antarctica. Solved.
But one sound has been out there since at least 1991... and NOAA still says its origin is unresolved. They call it Upsweep.

listen.label: "UPSWEEP"  ·  UNEXPLAINED
listen.credit: Audio: NOAA PMEL Acoustics Program / public domain

lines.text: It's loud enough to be heard across the Pacific. It rises and falls with the seasons. And NOAA says it can still be detected today.
Something down there is still making that sound. Comment Bloop... if you think it's alive.
